stages.name: Globalisation, trade patterns and RTAs
stages.title: Globalisation, trade patterns and RTAs
stages.sub: After this you can explain how globalisation creates inequality, how emerging economies reshape trade, and why trade agreements attract investment.

steps.q: A country opens up to trade. Its exporters boom and hire more staff, but its firms that competed with cheap imports shut down and lay off staff. Does globalisation help everyone in the country equally?
steps.right: No, some gain and some lose out
steps.wrong: Yes, growth means everyone benefits the same
steps.hint: Think about the exporters versus the firms facing new import competition.

steps.hint: One group's skills are now in higher demand than before; the other group faces more competition.

steps.q: Some countries and workers ride the export boom, others lose out to import competition, and skilled workers pull further ahead of unskilled ones. Does globalisation spread the gains evenly, between countries and within them?
steps.right: No, gaps widen both between and within countries
steps.hint: Combine the country-level winners/losers with the skilled/unskilled wage gap.

steps.q: A country with very low wages builds huge factories and starts making most of the world's phones and clothes, taking this production away from higher-wage countries. Does world manufacturing stay spread out the same way as before?
steps.right: No, it shifts towards the low-wage producer
steps.wrong: Yes, production stays evenly spread as before
steps.hint: Where would firms rather build factories if labour is much cheaper in one place?

steps.q: As manufacturing concentrates in low-wage countries, and gains from trade split unevenly between rich and poor nations, do the goods that each type of country exports and imports stay the same as 50 years ago?
steps.right: No, who exports what has changed a lot
steps.wrong: Yes, the same countries still export the same goods
steps.hint: Think about a country that used to import manufactured goods now exporting them instead.

steps.q: A UK firm builds a factory in Vietnam to run the business itself, rather than just buying a few Vietnamese shares. Is this the same as an investor briefly buying and selling shares abroad?
steps.right: No, it's a lasting stake in running a foreign business
steps.wrong: Yes, both are just buying foreign shares
steps.hint: One is building and controlling operations abroad; the other is trading paper assets.

steps.q: Two countries sign a deal removing tariffs between them permanently. Can a firm building a factory in one country now be confident its goods will reach the other country's customers tariff-free for years to come?
steps.right: Yes, the deal locks in that access
steps.wrong: No, access could disappear at any time
